articles.title: Immunogenicity risk assessment of novel modalities using new approach methodologies.
articles.abstract: A new generation of medicines that includes gene therapies, cell-based treatments and gene editors have the potential to treat a vast range of diseases. However, the clinical success of these novel modalities is limited by unwanted immune responses, which can compromise both safety and efficacy. Regulatory agencies have recently emphasized reducing animal testing in preclinical safety studies and envisioned a strategic approach for basing regulatory decisions on scientifically validated new approach methodologies (NAMs). These methods encompass mathematical models, artificial intelligence tools, organ-on-a-chip systems, and advanced in vitro and ex vivo assays. In combination, these approaches seem potentially well suited for assessing unwanted immune responses of the novel modalities. Key challenges to be addressed include predicting the immunogenicity risks from transgene products, delivery vehicles and gene-editing machinery; managing pre-existing immunity; overcoming barriers to repeat dosing; and establishing robust long-term monitoring strategies. In this Perspective, we critically evaluate how the current NAMs toolkit, originally developed for protein therapeutics, can be adapted to assess the unwanted immune responses of novel modalities. We provide a forward-looking framework for developing and validating the next generation of predictive immunogenicity tools required to safely unlock the full therapeutic potential of these revolutionary medicines.

articles.title: Emerging HER2-targeted treatment approaches for gastroesophageal cancer in the era of chemo-immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a key therapeutic target in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA) and its targeting agents form the backbone of treatment for HER2-positive disease. Therapeutic options have expanded from the HER2-targeting antibody trastuzumab to antibody-drug conjugates (ADC). HER2-directed small-molecule inhibitors and bispecific HER2-directed compounds are under evaluation in treatment-naive and previously treated patients across different stages of disease. Beyond combinations with chemotherapy, combinations with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are of particular interest due to potential synergistic mechanisms, including antigen release, immune-cell recruitment, and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity resulting in enhanced antitumor immunity. The current standard of care for HER2- and PD-L1-positive metastatic GEA (mGEA) combines chemotherapy with the HER2-targeting antibody trastuzumab and the PD-1-targeting ICI pembrolizumab. In the second-line setting, the ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan has further improved outcomes for these patients. Despite these advances and the emergence of new therapeutic options, several challenges remain, including optimal patient and drug selection, treatment sequencing, and the management of acquired resistance. Advances in liquid biopsy approaches, including the analysis of circulating tumor DNA, may facilitate longitudinal disease monitoring and guide personalized treatment strategies. This review summarizes the current and evolving role of HER2-targeted therapies in GEA, examines the growing integration of immunotherapy, and discusses future directions.

articles.title: Toward precision nanomedicine via artificial intelligence guided design and prediction.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing nanomedicine development by linking formulation variables and biological context with delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and safety. This review examines AI assisted formulation design, centralized formulation databases, prediction of nanoparticle self assembly, and models of cell and tissue selective delivery, biodistribution, and therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in predicting nanotoxicity and nanoparticle induced immune responses further emphasize the importance of incorporating safety endpoints into nanomedicine optimization. Beyond nanocarrier engineering, foundation models and multimodal analyses of single-cell and spatial data are expanding biological discovery by characterizing disease associated cellular states, prioritizing therapeutic targets, and predicting treatment responses. Computational approaches also support the design of therapeutic RNA, peptides, proteins, and programmable protein nanomaterials. For example, mRNA sequences generated by GEMORNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles increased erythropoietin expression in mice by up to 15-fold compared with a benchmark sequence. Integration of biological discovery with biomolecular and nanocarrier design may inform therapeutic cargo selection, targeting strategies, and functional nanomaterial development. AI may connect patient specific biological characteristics with predictions of nanomedicine delivery and therapeutic response to support patient stratification and individualized treatment selection. Integration of histological, imaging, molecular, and longitudinal data may enable treatment strategies to be adapted to differences in tissue characteristics, disease state, and therapeutic response. Emerging approaches based on digital twins and adaptive treatment control may extend the framework toward individualized dosing and dynamic treatment optimization. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, limited model generalizability, and the need for experimental and prospective validation. Progress toward precision therapy will require integrated frameworks that jointly consider delivery, efficacy, selectivity, and safety while clearly distinguishing demonstrated applications from future opportunities.

articles.title: Stromal Immune Niches in Transplantation: Signaling Circuits and Therapeutic Targets beyond Lymphoid Organs.
articles.abstract: Stromal cells, the extracellular matrix (ECM), and vascular and lymphatic networks are increasingly recognized as organizers of local immune responses in solid organ grafts. However, transplant immunology remains centered largely on immune cells and lymphoid tissues. Here we propose the graft stromal immune niche as an operational concept: a spatially restricted microenvironment in which local stromal, vascular, lymphatic, or matrix-derived cues are associated with measurable changes in immune-cell localization, persistence, differentiation, or function. Synthesizing evidence from kidney, heart, lung, and liver grafts, we describe three recurring spatial contexts-perivascular, interface-associated, and perilymphatic/egress-associated-and discuss how early injury, ECM mechanics, and stromal programming may shape niche behavior over time. Building on current evidence, we propose a three-state model encompassing rejection-prone, tolerance-permissive, and fibrotic niches; delineate established knowledge and remaining evidence gaps; and critically evaluate pharmacological interventions at different stages of clinical development. This framework is intended to guide the interpretation of spatial datasets and the design of niche-directed strategies.

articles.title: Bacteria-inspired drug delivery systems for cancer immunotherapy: from exploiting to mimicking.
articles.abstract: Bacteria possess distinctive properties, including preferential tumor colonization, motility, immune stimulation, and genetic tractability, which provide opportunities for drug delivery and cancer immunotherapy. These properties have supported the development of living bacteria-based delivery systems that transport therapeutic cargo, produce therapeutic agents locally, and regulate antitumor immune responses. Herein, we review the therapeutic mechanisms and design strategies of these systems, focusing on how bacterial natural characteristics enhance delivery efficiency, enable cargo loading, and control in situ therapeutic production and release. We also discuss how administration routes influence their delivery performance and therapeutic outcomes. Building on these advances, we examine bacteria-inspired biomimetic delivery systems that reproduce selected bacterial structures and functions, including morphology, surface recognition and adhesion, and navigation mechanisms. By combining these features with defined materials, biomimetic systems may improve targeting and tissue penetration while reducing replication-associated infection risks and improving control over composition and immune stimulation. Finally, we compare the capabilities and limitations of living bacterial platforms and biomimetic systems and discuss their distinct safety concerns and translational requirements. This review connects the exploitation of living bacterial characteristics with biomimetic design and identifies priorities for developing bacteria-inspired cancer immunotherapies.

articles.title: Natural products as modulators of the NLRP3 inflammasome: mechanisms of action, chemical diversity, and therapeutic potential.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome is a cytosolic multiprotein signaling platform that coordinates caspase-1 activation, interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18 maturation, and pyroptosis following infection or tissue injury. Its dysregulation contributes to diverse inflammatory diseases. Natural products offer structurally diverse scaffolds for NLRP3 modulator discovery. PURPOSE: This review evaluates natural products that inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, with emphasis on their chemical diversity, direct and indirect mechanisms, structure-activity relationships, and translational limitations. METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception through July, 2026 using combinations of "NLRP3" with "natural compounds", "traditional Chinese medicine", or "Chinese herbal medicine". Manual screening identified 46 structurally defined compounds with experimental evidence of NLRP3 regulation. Clinical trial registries were searched through July 2026 for NLRP3-targeting agents in clinical development. RESULTS: The 46 natural compounds comprised alkaloids, terpenoids, flavonoids, and phenolic compounds. Their reported mechanisms included direct engagement of NLRP3, interference with NLRP3-NEK7-dependent inflammasome assembly, and indirect modulation of NF-κB-dependent priming, oxidative and mitochondrial stress, ion fluxes, autophagy, and mitophagy. Direct target engagement was supported for only a limited subset, whereas most compounds acted through upstream pathways. Clinical development was dominated by synthetic inhibitors, while clinical validation of natural-product-derived NLRP3 modulators remained limited. CONCLUSION: Natural products represent a promising source of NLRP3 inflammasome modulators and lead scaffolds for anti-inflammatory drug discovery. Further studies should establish target engagement and selectivity, characterize pharmacokinetic and safety profiles, and validate efficacy in clinically relevant models to support clinical translation.

articles.title: Drug Repurposing in Pre-Eclampsia: Maternal Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic Considerations for Clinical Trial Design.
articles.abstract: Pre-eclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy affecting 3-8% of pregnancies worldwide, with no disease-modifying therapy currently available. Drug repurposing offers a promising strategy, yet no candidate has been validated to date. Pregnancy-associated physiological changes alter drug pharmacokinetics (PK), and pre-eclampsia itself may further modify drug disposition, complicating dose selection and contributing to inconclusive clinical trial outcomes. A structured literature search identified six prospective or randomized controlled trials of repurposed drugs for established pre-eclampsia: esomeprazole, omeprazole, sulfasalazine, pravastatin, recombinant antithrombin, and metformin. All drugs were well tolerated, with metformin the one to show promising clinical benefit by prolonging gestation; the remaining five drugs yielded inconclusive or null efficacy outcomes. Critically, PK sampling was conducted in only three trials, and none systematically characterized exposure-response relationships using key pre-eclampsia biomarkers, including soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, soluble endoglin, and placental growth factor. Further common methodological limitations included small sample sizes (12-120 participants), heterogeneous gestational age eligibility criteria, and dosing regimens extrapolated from non-pregnant populations without pregnancy-specific optimization. These shortcomings likely contributed to the translational gap between promising preclinical findings and positive clinical trial outcomes. Model-informed drug development (MIDD) approaches, including physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) and population pharmacokinetic (popPK) modeling, optimal sampling strategies, and simulation-based dose selection, offer a framework to improve pre-eclampsia trial design. Future studies should integrate these approaches with biomarker-guided exposure-response analyses and prediction of fetal exposure throughout pregnancy to enhance therapeutic development, optimize maternal-fetal safety, and accelerate the identification of effective disease-modifying therapies for pre-eclampsia.

articles.title: Pharmacogenomic Determinants of Asparaginase-Induced Hypersensitivity, Pancreatitis, Thrombosis, and Hepatotoxicity in Children: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Asparaginase is a common treatment for childhood hematological malignancies, but its use may be limited by toxicities including hypersensitivity, pancreatitis, thrombosis, and hepatotoxicity. Pharmacogenomic testing may identify children who are genetically predisposed to these toxicities, thus enabling personalized treatment. We performed a systematic review to synthesize and critically appraise available evidence for pharmacogenomic associations with asparaginase-induced toxicities in pediatric oncology patients. Literature searches of MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were performed to identify studies investigating genetic associations with asparaginase-induced hypersensitivity, pancreatitis, thrombosis, or hepatotoxicity in children. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment using the Q-GENIE tool were performed independently by two reviewers. Forty studies met inclusion criteria. Evidence was the strongest for hypersensitivity, with consistent replication of associations involving HLA class II alleles, particularly the HLA-DRB1*07:01-HLA-DQA1*02:01-HLA-DQB1*02:02 haplotype, although risk alleles differed by ancestry. For hepatotoxicity, evidence was limited to three studies, but PNPLA3 rs738409 was identified and independently replicated. Associations with pancreatitis and thrombosis were heterogeneous, with numerous candidate loci reported but limited validation across independent cohorts. The overall evidence base was highly heterogeneous, characterized by varying toxicity definitions, inconsistent reporting of statistical power, and limited replication. Current evidence supports HLA class II alleles and PNPLA3 as the most promising pharmacogenomic markers of asparaginase hypersensitivity and hepatotoxicity respectively, but larger, ancestrally diverse studies with standardized toxicity definitions and independent validation are required before routine clinical implementation.

articles.title: New anti-inflammatory and remodelling drugs for unmet clinical needs in severe asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
articles.abstract: There have been several step-changes in asthma therapy, with the first being the use of inhaled short-acting β2-agonists as bronchodilators and the introduction of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) to reduce airway inflammation. The next revolution was the advent of inhaled combinations of long-acting bronchodilators together with inhaled corticosteroids in the same inhalation device for improved asthma control. The most recent step-change is the introduction of targeted monoclonal antibodies in patients with severe asthma and frequent exacerbations with biomarkers reflecting high levels of Type 2 (T2) inflammation. In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), advances in bronchodilator therapy have been made, but limited advances in treating the inflammation and lung remodelling changes are present. We need new therapeutic agents for patients with a sub-optimal response to current drugs. The aim of this narrative review is to provide a summary of the potential future anti-inflammatory approaches undergoing testing for asthma and COPD rather than provide a systematic review. These approaches aim to optimize current treatment regimens and to develop novel agents against differing aspects of asthma and COPD pathophysiology. However, clinical trial results highlight our limited understanding of the biology of asthma and COPD subtypes. Furthermore, failed studies provide insight into disease pathophysiology and may indicate responder/non-responder populations. Various aspects of cytokine- and environment-activated intracellular pathways are being targeted. These include receptor agonists and antagonists and inhibitors of the Janus kinase (JAK) and Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) pathways for use against both stable disease and for reducing disease exacerbations or 'attacks'. New or better use of current biomarkers will provide non-invasive means of patients most likely to respond to any one specific or combination of drugs.

articles.title: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for HIV: a meta-analysis of efficacy across treatment-naïve and experienced populations and comparative effectiveness versus dolutegravir/lamivudine.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (BIC/FTC/TAF) is a preferred single-tablet regimen for HIV treatment, but head-to-head meta-analytic comparisons between treatment-experienced (TE) and treatment-naïve (TN) individuals are lacking. Additionally, the comparative effectiveness of BIC/FTC/TAF versus dolutegravir/lamivudine (DTG/3TC) remains to be systematically synthesized. We aimed to systematically compare the efficacy of BIC/FTC/TAF between TE and TN people with HIV, and evaluate the comparative effectiveness of BIC/FTC/TAF versus DTG/3TC. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase up to September 2026. Observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reporting virologic suppression or treatment discontinuation rates in both TE and TN populations receiving BIC/FTC/TAF, or BIC/FTC/TAF versus DTG/3TC were included. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Single-group proportion meta-analyses used a random-effects model, whereas comparative meta-analyses used the prespecified fixed-effect model. RESULTS: Thirty-one studies were included. For TE participants, the pooled virologic suppression rate was 95% (95% CI: 92%-97%) at 12 months, and for TN participants, the rate was 90% (95% CI: 85%-94%). In design-stratified comparative analyses between BIC/FTC/TAF and DTG/3TC, no statistically significant difference was detected in RCT (OR = 1.46, 95% CI: 0.80-2.66) or cohort studies (OR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.70-1.39) among TN populations, nor in TE populations (RCT: OR = 1.04, 95% CI: 0.34-3.16; cohort: OR = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.42-2.02). No statistically significant differences were detected for treatment discontinuation (all-cause: OR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.70-1.49; adverse events: OR = 1.11, 95% CI: 0.55-2.22). CONCLUSION: BIC/FTC/TAF achieves high virologic suppression rates and low discontinuation rates in both TE and TN populations, supporting its use as a first-line and switch option. BIC/FTC/TAF and DTG/3TC showed no statistically significant differences in virologic suppression or treatment discontinuation, suggesting both are viable guideline-preferred options. The choice between them should be individualized based on patient characteristics, including prior treatment history, adherence potential, comorbidity profile, and metabolic risk considerations.

articles.title: Differing roles of the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and amylin receptors in migraine-related light aversion and gastrointestinal dysfunction in mice.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The neuropeptide calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a well-established player in migraine. Current CGRP migraine therapeutics were designed to inhibit the canonical CGRP receptor, yet, based on in vitro studies, they can also inhibit to a lesser degree the amylin receptor 1 (AMY1), which CGRP can also activate. This study explores the potential in vivo contributions of these receptors to migraine-like symptoms in mice. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Receptor contributions were probed using light aversion as a surrogate for photophobia and diarrhoea as a readout for gastrointestinal dysfunction in outbred CD1 mice. Induction of diarrhoea was also measured in C57BL/6 J mice. CGRP and amylin were used as agonists, with two selective antagonists, olcegepant for the canonical CGRP receptor and AC187 for calcitonin receptor (CT)-based receptors, including AMY1. KEY RESULTS: CGRP and amylin induced light aversion in CD1 mice and diarrhoea in both strains. CGRP-induced light aversion was partially rescued by AC187, but not olcegepant. Light aversion was fully rescued only by a combination of AC187 and olcegepant. In contrast, olcegepant fully blocked CGRP-induced diarrhoea, while AC187 only partially blocked at high doses. As a control, olcegepant fully rescued CGRP-induced periorbital touch hypersensitivity in CD1 mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: More than one receptor contributes to CGRP-induced light aversion, with a CT-based receptor unexpectedly playing a major role. In contrast, the canonical CGRP receptor plays a major role in CGRP-induced diarrhoea. Thus, targeting a CT-based receptor may reduce photophobia with less adverse gastrointestinal effects in migraine patients.

articles.title: Cancer vaccine development gets complicated.
How can gene therapy platforms be scaled up to treat thousands of rare diseases?
Hypoxia-responsive CAIX-targeted radioligand for non-invasive imaging and radioligand therapy: from preclinical to first-in-human evaluation.
articles.abstract: Carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) is an attractive target for radioligand theranostics because it is constitutively overexpressed in clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and induced by hypoxia in several solid tumors. Existing CAIX-targeted radiotracers are constrained by delayed imaging kinetics, limited tumor retention, incomplete therapeutic-labeling compatibility, or insufficient tumor-to-background contrast. Here we report GL-261, a CAIX-targeted radioligand that appends a nitroimidazole bioreductive retention module to a CAIX-targeting pharmacophore within a DOTA-chelated scaffold. This design enables paired radiolabeling with gallium-68 for PET imaging and lutetium-177 for radioligand therapy. Nitroimidazole conjugation conferred hypoxia-dependent cellular accumulation, greater internalization (64.6% versus 45.2%), and higher CAIX-dependent tumor uptake than the comparator DPI-4452 without compromising target specificity. In xenograft models spanning different CAIX expression levels, [68Ga]Ga-GL-261 PET stratified tumors by CAIX status and was suppressed by receptor blocking. [177Lu]Lu-GL-261 showed sustained tumor retention over 168h and, at 37 MBq, produced marked tumor growth suppression without overt hematological or organ toxicity. In a first-in-human PET/CT study of 15 patients, [68Ga]Ga-GL-261 showed reproducible biodistribution, an effective dose of 8.45 × 10-2mSv/MBq, and lesion uptake that correlated with CAIX immunohistochemical expression (r = 0.93, P = 0.007 at 60min). These findings support hypoxia-responsive modification as a design strategy for CAIX-targeted radioligands and provide a translational basis for GL-261 in CAIX-expressing cancers. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trail (registration No. ChiCTR2600127500).

articles.title: Targeting the SND1-MTDH/FANCD2 axis impairs DNA repair and sensitizes triple-negative breast cancer to PARP inhibitor.
articles.abstract: Although the staphylococcal nuclease domain-containing protein 1 (SND1)-metadherin (MTDH) complex is a promising therapeutic target in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), its role in DNA damage repair (DDR) remains unclear. Here, we identified FANCD2 as a previously unrecognized downstream effector of the SND1-MTDH complex. SND1 and MTDH cooperate to stabilize FANCD2 mRNA, thereby sustaining FANCD2 expression and DDR in TNBC cells. Guided by our finding, we designed DP3, an MTDH-derived peptide inhibitor that binds SND1 with high affinity and selectively disrupts the SND1-MTDH interaction. DP3 promoted degradation of both SND1 and MTDH, destabilized FANCD2 mRNA, reduced FANCD2 expression, and consequently increased DNA damage accumulation. Functionally, DP3 suppressed TNBC cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and survival and showed potent antitumor activity in patient-derived organoids and xenograft models, with a favorable safety profile in vivo. Importantly, DP3 enhanced the antitumor activity of PARP inhibitors (PARPi) in TNBC models by further suppressing FANCD2 expression and promoting DNA damage accumulation. These findings identify the SND1-MTDH/FANCD2 axis as a previously unrecognized regulator of DDR and PARPi sensitivity and provide a rationale for combining SND1-MTDH interaction inhibitors with PARPi in TNBC.

articles.title: An oral delivery platform for protein drugs: PDA/PEGylated engineered probiotics responsively release TLR5 agonists to prevent radiation enteritis.
articles.abstract: Oral protein delivery is hindered by gastrointestinal degradation and poor mucosal bioavailability. Engineered probiotics offer a promising strategy for oral protein delivery, but their therapeutic efficacy is often limited by insufficient payload expression and low secretion efficiency. Here, we present a living oral platform that integrates high-yield protein biosynthesis with on-demand intestinal release. By gene manipulation and FLAG tagging, we dramatically upregulate constitutive expression of GP532 in probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), while installing an arabinose-inducible autolytic switch for efficient intracellular payload release. A dual-layer coating of polydopamine (PDA) and polyethylene glycol (PEG) confers acid resistance and mucus penetration, while allowing arabinose to permeate and blocking digestive enzymes. Upon single oral gavage in a murine model of radiation enteritis, our formulation achieves therapeutic efficacy fully equivalent to systemic injection of GP532 in mitigating intestinal injury. Critically, unlike injectable biologics, this living platform promotes the restoration of gut microbial community structure and beneficial taxa, a unique benefit unattainable by parenteral administration, while the engineered strain is completely cleared within 24 h. By synergizing genetic circuit engineering, surface chemical modification, and in situ luminal release, this work establishes a single-dose, orally effective alternative to injectable protein therapy, offering a transformative strategy for the prevention of radiation enteritis with the added benefit of microbiome maintenance.

articles.title: Dissolving microneedle patches for needle-free and thermostable respiratory syncytial virus vaccination.
articles.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of acute lower respiratory tract disease, yet current prefusion F (preF)-based RSV vaccines depend on intramuscular injection and cold-chain distribution, limiting broad deployment. Dissolving microneedle array patches (MAPs) offer a minimally invasive, needle-free, and potentially thermostable alternative to conventional vaccine delivery. Here, we developed dissolving microneedle array patches loaded with an engineered prefusion-stabilized RSV F antigen (CL073A) and evaluated their potential as a needle-free, thermostable, and potent RSV vaccination platform. Following formulation screening, two lead CL073A-loaded MAPs (MAPs-CL073A) were identified that preserved antigenicity and mechanical performance and showed prolonged local antigen retention relative to intramuscular injection. In mice, MAPs-CL073A elicited markedly enhanced and durable humoral immunity, inducing approximately five-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers than intramuscular immunization at a ten-fold lower antigen dose, demonstrating a pronounced dose-sparing effect. In cotton rats, MAPs-CL073A conferred robust protection against RSV challenge by reducing lung viral burden and pulmonary pathology, with the 10 μg regimen (F2-MAP) achieving near-complete protection. Furthermore, the patches fully retained antigen bioactivity and in vivo immunogenicity after 6 months of room-temperature storage. Our findings establish that antigen delivery is a critical dimension of RSV vaccine performance and support dissolving microneedle delivery as a versatile strategy to enhance both the efficacy and deployability of RSV vaccines.

articles.title: Copper dysregulation and ferroptotic vulnerability in Wilson disease: Mechanistic evidence and therapeutic potential of plant-derived natural compounds.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: ATP7B dysfunction in Wilson disease (WD) disrupts copper homeostasis and promotes mitochondrial injury, altered iron handling, and oxidative lipid damage. Whether these changes culminate in ferroptotic cell death, and whether plant-derived compounds provide ferroptosis-dependent protection, remain unresolved. PURPOSE: To critically examine the mechanistic basis of ferroptotic vulnerability in WD and assess the evidence and translational potential of chemically defined plant-derived compounds. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception through 16 September 2026. Eligible experimental studies were assessed for methodological limitations and disease-model fidelity, and mechanistic evidence was graded using a review-specific cumulative four-level framework. Findings were synthesized narratively alongside contextual mechanistic, pharmacokinetic, and safety literature. RESULTS: Seven preclinical studies evaluating curcumin, ferulic acid, diosgenin, berberine, aloe-emodin, quercetin, and polydatin were included. Reported protection in hepatic, neural, or ovarian models was accompanied by changes in copper handling, antioxidant defenses, and lipid metabolism. Six studies remained at Level 1 (ferroptosis-compatible evidence); only the polydatin study reached Level 2, providing functional pharmacological support with nonspecific endpoints. No study met the criteria for dependence on core ferroptosis machinery or convergent causal validation (Levels 3 and 4), and functional validation in human WD-derived systems was absent. Protection specifically attributable to ferroptosis suppression at matched copper burden remained unproven. Uncertain target-organ exposure and insufficient long-term safety and combination-treatment data further constrain translation. CONCLUSION: Plant-derived compounds warrant investigation as potential adjuncts to established copper-lowering therapy, but their ferroptosis-specific mechanisms and clinical benefit in WD remain unestablished. Copper-matched mechanistic studies, independent replication, and pharmacokinetic and safety evaluation are required to determine whether they offer additional organ protection.

articles.title: Pyrithiones induce cytotoxicity via NADPH oxidase 1-dependent oxidative zinc release in rat vascular smooth muscle cells.
articles.abstract: Pyrithiones are antimicrobial biocides that are also widely used as experimental zinc ionophores. Despite their well-established biocidal activity, their biological and toxicological effects in mammalian cells remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cytotoxic mechanisms of sodium pyrithione (NaPT) and related pyrithiones in primary cultured vascular smooth muscle cells. Unexpectedly, 0.1-10 µM NaPT markedly increased cytosolic free Zn2+ within 10 min, even in the absence of extracellular Zn2+. Prolonged exposure induced pronounced cytotoxicity, which was completely abolished by the Zn2+ chelator TPEN, demonstrating that this toxicity depends on cytosolic Zn2+. NaPT also depleted intracellular thiols, whereas the membrane-permeable thiol donor glutathione ethyl ester (GSH-EE) prevented this depletion and the cytosolic Zn2+ elevation, indicating that the Zn2+ elevation is thiol-dependent, likely reflecting the release of Zn2+ from zinc-thiolate motifs in intracellular proteins. Mechanistically, NaPT stimulated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which was suppressed by the NADPH oxidase (NOX) inhibitors DPI and GKT137831, knockdown of p22phox and NOX1, the PKC inhibitor GF109203X, the PKCβ-selective inhibitor LY333531, and Ca2+ depletion using cyclopiazonic acid. These interventions, together with the superoxide scavenger TEMPOL, also prevented NaPT-induced thiol depletion and Zn2+ elevation. Furthermore, NaPT-induced cytotoxicity was attenuated by DPI and GKT137831, NOX1 knockdown, TEMPOL, and GSH-EE. Similar results were obtained with zinc pyrithione and copper pyrithione. Collectively, pyrithiones induce cytotoxicity through a signaling cascade involving PKCβ activation, NOX1-mediated ROS generation, oxidative disruption of protein zinc-thiolate complexes, and cytosolic Zn2+ mobilization. This cascade operates independently of extracellular Zn2+ influx, revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism underlying pyrithione-induced cytotoxicity in mammalian cells.

articles.title: Defining the normal pharmacogenomic/toxicogenomic phenotype for N-acetyltransferase 2.
articles.abstract: The aim of this paper is to consider the ramifications of defining "normal" in the context of an individual's pharmacogenomic/toxicogenomic phenotype, referencing recent reports of the International N-Acetyltransferase Workshop published in Archives of Toxicology and the clinical function assignment of N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) alleles and metabolizer phenotypes by the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) Pharmacogene Curation Expert Panel published in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics. As outlined in the paper, numerous pharmacogenomic/toxicogenomic applications justify enthusiastic endorsement of the recent decision by the CPIC expert panel to assign three NAT2 phenotypic categories of rapid, intermediate, and poor metabolizers, avoiding the "normal metabolizer" category. Similarly, these applications justify the CPIC expert panel NAT2 allele assignments of increased, decreased, or unknown function avoiding assignment of any NAT2 allele as "normal function."

articles.title: In vitro human hepatocyte incubation of 5F-MDMB-PINACA, 5F-MDMB-PICA, 5F-EMDB-PICA, 4F-MDMB-BICA, and 4F-MDMB-BINACA and cannabinoid receptor 1 activity profiling of major human metabolites.
articles.abstract: Since their first reported fatalities in 2016, fluorinated MDMB-group synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists (SCRAs), 5F-MDMB-PINACA, 5F-MDMB-PICA, 5F-EDMB-PICA, 4F-MDMB-BICA, and 4F-MDMB-BINACA, have remained present on illegal drug markets. Detection of SCRAs in clinical and forensic casework relies on metabolite detection, yet confirmation using metabolite reference standards is often lacking. Moreover, limited knowledge is available regarding the metabolites' activity at the cannabinoid 1 receptor (CB1) and their potential contribution to cannabinoid pharmacology and toxicology. Therefore, this work aimed to confirm major metabolites of the five analogue SCRAs using in-house-synthesized reference standards and evaluate their activity at the CB1 receptor. SCRAs (5 µM) were incubated for 3 h with human hepatocytes, and supernatants were analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography coupled to quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (HPLC-QToF-MS), and spectra were compared with reference standards. Parent and metabolite activity were measured using an in vitro recombinant cell AequoScreen® assay with a concentration range of 0.0286 nM-60 µM. Sixteen of 20 assessed metabolites were confirmed, including major metabolites such as ester hydrolysis (EH), carboxylic acid formation, combinations with oxidative defluorination (OD). Ten major and rapidly formed metabolites, such as hydroxylated metabolites, OD, and EH, showed high to moderate CB1 potency (EC50 96.3 nM-8.07 µM), whereas metabolites with multiple biotransformations showed little to no activation. Together, this study confirms several major metabolites using reference standards and characterizes their CB1 activity, improving confidence in SCRA detection and providing insight into metabolite contribution to cannabinoid-related activity.

articles.title: Fungicide-induced developmental and reproductive toxicity in rodents: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Fungicides are extensively used in agriculture; however, growing evidence suggests potential adverse effects on reproductive and developmental processes in non-target organisms. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate maternal fungicide exposure effects on reproductive and fetal outcomes in rodent models. A systematic literature search from 2000 to 2024 was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect following PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies assessed implantation, resorption, post-implantation loss, fetal viability, and congenital anomalies. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using inverse-variance and Mantel-Haenszel methods. Fourteen studies were included. Fungicide exposure was associated with increased resorption rates and post-implantation loss, as well as a reduction in live fetuses. Meta-analytical estimates also demonstrated significantly increased risks for congenital anomalies, including external, visceral and skeletal malformations with consistent effects across multiple fungicide classes. Subgroup analyses indicated that the toxicity varied according to fungicide class, dose, and exposure duration, with triazole and imidazole compounds showing the most consistent adverse effects. Overall, the findings demonstrate that maternal fungicide exposure induces significant reproductive and developmental toxicity in rodents, supporting mechanisms involving endocrine disruption and embryotoxicity.

articles.title: How robust are transcriptomics-based points of departure when translated to in vivo doses by kinetic-modeling? A case study with the herbicide pendimethalin using HepG2 and HepaRG cells.
articles.abstract: Risk assessment of agrochemicals has traditionally relied on animal studies to derive points of departure (PODs) for the establishment of regulatory guidance values. More recently, new approach methodologies (NAMs) have been explored as a means to estimate protective exposure levels without generating new animal data. In the present case study, we evaluated whether a transcriptomics-based NAM workflow combined with physiologically-based kinetic (PBK) modeling can provide biologically plausible estimates of systemic toxicity thresholds for pendimethalin (PDM), an agrochemical with extensive toxicological and kinetic reference data. We compared two in vitro liver models and transcriptomic approaches: targeted TempO-Seq in HepG2 cells and untargeted RNA sequencing in HepaRG cells. After 48 h exposure to PDM in concentration ranges of 0.07-202 µM (HepaRG) and 0.8-56 µM (HepG2), gene expression changes were analyzed using benchmark-dose modeling in BMDExpress 3.0. Transcriptomic PODs (tPODs) were derived using gene- and distribution-based approaches and subsequently translated to external doses by in vitro-to-in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) employing three rat PBK models. The resulting PODs were compared with regulatory in vivo PODs reported for PDM. In addition, a human population-based PBK model was used to derive an oral equivalent dose (OED) from the most sensitive transcriptomic POD. Across transcriptomic platforms, tPOD derivation methods, and PBK models, the resulting IVIVE-derived PODs generally fell within the range of regulatory in vivo PODs reported for PDM. The most sensitive prediction yielded a POD of 6.0 mg/kg bw/day for the rat, while human population-based modeling resulted in a 5th-percentile OED of 0.068 mg/kg bw/day, close to currently established regulatory guidance values. Notably, the variability introduced by the choice of toxicokinetic model was of a similar magnitude as the variability associated with transcriptomic POD derivation, indicating that uncertainty in IVIVE contributes at least as much to the final prediction as uncertainty in transcriptomic data analysis. Overall, this study supports the feasibility of combining in vitro transcriptomics with IVIVE to estimate systemic toxicity thresholds for an agrochemical compound. The results encourage further evaluation of transcriptomics-based NAM workflows and next-generation risk assessment of agrochemicals. Assessment of a broader range of agrochemicals, together with continued refinement of toxicokinetic modeling and in vitro dosimetry, will be required to establish their predictive performance and future regulatory applicability.

articles.title: Mitochondrial DNA-cGAS-STING induces macrophage pyroptosis via phospho-IRF3-mediated NLRP3 expression in ionising radiation-induced atherosclerosis progression.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Ionising radiation (IR) is a major cancer-treatment modality, yet the mechanisms driving IR-triggered cardiovascular injury are poorly defined. This work aimed to uncover how IR accelerates atherosclerosis (AS) and the underlying molecular mechanisms. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: We applied 9.4 T magnetic resonance imaging to evaluate atherosclerotic lesions. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on carotid arteries. Apolipoprotein E (ApoE) knockout mice with caspase-1 deletion and macrophage-specific cGAS knockdown were used for in vivo validation. JASPAR prediction and dual-luciferase reporter assays were implemented to verify transcriptional regulation of NLRP3. KEY RESULTS: IR substantially aggravated atherosclerotic progression, accompanied by elevated pyroptosis-related gene expression in macrophages within atherosclerotic plaques. Mechanistically, IR promoted cytoplasmic mtDNA release to activate the cGAS/STING/TBK1 axis and cause p-IRF3 nuclear translocation. Phosphorylated IRF3 bound to the NLRP3 promoter and enhanced its transcription. Genetic ablation of caspase-1 or macrophage-specific cGAS knockdown alleviated IR-driven AS progression. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: Macrophage pyroptosis drives IR-accelerated AS progression through the mtDNA/cGAS/STING/p-IRF3 axis-dependent transcriptional up-regulation of NLRP3. Targeting the cGAS-STING pathway may provide a therapeutic strategy for IR-associated atherosclerotic plaque progression.

articles.title: Identifying Pediatric and Developmental Screening Targets With Biologically Informed Molecular Representations.
articles.abstract: More than 75% of Food and Drug Administration approved drugs lack pediatric dosing, efficacy, or safety data, and roughly 40% of medications prescribed to children are used off-label. For most therapies children receive, dose, formulation, or indication has never been formally evaluated in anyone under 18. In this work, we build on our previous model, BioMADE, to identify toxicity screening targets whose relevance is specific to defined developmental stages. We analyzed 3.8 million drug-condition records from KidSIDES across 7 developmental stages and 6 system organ classes. Univariate analysis identified biologically coherent genes associated with pediatric conditions, including known genes like GABRB1 (pathogenic variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy), SLC6A1 (associated with developmental encephalopathies), and GRIN2A (defining gene of epilepsy-aphasia spectrum). Signals were the strongest in early life, spanning multiple organ systems. The highest univariate model was gene CTSS, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.776; 95% confidence interval 0.62-0.90. Multivariate models surpassed 0.8 area under receiving operator curve in 13 datasets (0.81-0.91), indicating that multi-gene drug interaction profiles carry predictive signal beyond single-target associations. We further identify secondary targets that may influence pediatric development and contribute to pediatric-specific adverse drug events, many of which are not included in current safety screening panels. Our findings support the development of novel pediatric-specific safety screening panels, with a particular emphasis on respiratory and congenital disorders in early life. Prioritizing relevant drug targets for pediatric screening can potentially reduce the challenges of pediatric clinical trials and advance safer, more precise pediatric drug therapies.

articles.title: Influence of genetic variants on the response to long-acting β2-agonists (LABAs) and long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) and combination therapies in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a heterogeneous respiratory disease in which patients may differ in terms of clinical course and response to drug treatment. Genetic variability may contribute to these differences by influencing drug response and clinical outcomes. This systematic review aimed to summarize the available evidence on the association between genetic variants and clinical outcomes or treatment response in patients with COPD receiving LABA- and/or LAMA-based therapies, as well as pharmacogenetic response to combination inhalants. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in the PubMed and Scopus databases, as well as in the gray literature, for studies published between 2015 and 2026. Studies were considered eligible if they included adults with COPD receiving LABA and/or LAMA treatment, including combination regimens, and evaluated genetic variants in relation to therapeutic response. Additionally, studies focusing on disease phenotypes rather than specific pharmacogenetic markers were also included. Study selection and data extraction were performed by two independent reviewers. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool. RESULTS: A total of 51 records were identified, and eight studies were included. Genetic variants in the ADRB2, FAM13A, SUMF1, MAPK8, AZU1, CSE1L, and CCL2 genes were investigated in relation to lung function, disease severity, and treatment response. ADRB2 variants (rs1042713, rs1042714, and rs1800888) were associated with lung function and exacerbation risk, although results regarding bronchodilator treatment response were inconsistent. Regarding other genetic variants, SUMF1 rs793391 emerged as a candidate variant in patients treated with combined bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). However, these findings are based on limited data and currently lack independent replication, warranting cautious interpretation. Furthermore, findings from large GWAS revealed novel candidates associated with treatment outcomes, though these results were not replicated in subsequent independent enome-Wide Association Study analyses. Due to the limited number of studies and considerable heterogeneity, no meta-analysis was performed. CONCLUSION: This review highlights the latest advances in COPD pharmacogenetics by synthesizing available evidence on patient responses to bronchodilators and corticosteroids. By mapping key methodological factors, the review provides valuable insight into optimizing future research. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420261392469.

articles.title: Hypothetico-Deductive Reasoning in Direct Oral Anticoagulant Trial Meta-Analyses: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) have become standard therapy for thrombosis prevention since 2008. Meta-analyses (MAs) of randomized controlled trials (RCT) are considered high-level evidence supporting clinical guidelines. However, methodological biases may yield false-positive findings, particularly through inadequate hypothesis formulation, multiple testing without alpha-risk correction, and selective outcome reporting. No study has systematically assessed the risk of false positives in MA evaluating DOAC through hypothetico-deductive reasoning. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess methodological features relevant to confirmatory inference in MA of RCTs evaluating DOACs, including hypothesis specification and multiplicity management, and to quantify nominal exposure to type I error under specified assumptions. METHODS: Following a pre-specified protocol, we conducted a meta-epidemiological study using embase and PubMed databases. We included MA of RCT evaluating four EMA-approved DOAC. Two independent authors performed study selection. For each MA, we calculated the nominal family-wise probability of at least one type I error under the global null hypothesis, assuming independent tests. We assessed the presence of directional hypotheses, primary outcome definition, pre-specified protocols, sensitivity analyses, and spin in conclusions. RESULTS: Ninety-three MA were included (mean 34 118 patients; seven RCT per MA). The median nominal family-wise type I error probability was 40%, and only 2.2% of MAs reported alpha-risk management, 26.9% had pre-specified protocols, and 14.0% reported directional hypotheses. Only 5.4% combined a clearly specified directional hypothesis with a single primary objective and well-defined outcome. Spin was present in 30.1% of conclusions. CONCLUSION: Most MAs showed substantial uncorrected nominal exposure to multiplicity; this estimate is a theoretical indicator and not the probability that a published conclusion is false. Many MAs also lacked explicit hypotheses and frequently exhibited spin. Strengthening reliability requires integrating genuine hypothetico-deductive approaches and adapting methodological guidelines.

Response to a letter to the editor entitled 'Long-acting relaxin for pulmonary hypertension: From systemic pharmacodynamics to disease-site pharmacology'.
The Role of Oxidative Stress and Antioxidant Signaling in Skin Wound Healing.
articles.abstract: Oxidative stress represents a prevalent form of cellular and tissue damage, arising from an imbalance between diminished antioxidant defense mechanisms and elevated reactive species production. This pathological condition occurs following exposure to endogenous or exogenous stressors, triggering the intracellular accumulation of excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), reactive nitrogen species (RNS), and other free radicals that ultimately induce cellular and tissue injury. Skin wounds are a disruption or interruption of normal skin anatomical organization and functional continuity. They can be categorized into acute and chronic skin wounds based on the time of healing, and consists of four overlapping stages: hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling phases. Any mistake in any stage can lead to delayed skin wound healing, non-healing ulcers or even scar formation, which happens especially easily in diabetic patients. Impaired skin wound repair represents a significant clinical concern that may precipitate severe sequelae such as localized soft tissue infection (cellulitis), tissue necrosis (gangrene), and systemic inflammatory response (sepsis). These complications frequently culminate in the necessity for surgical limb amputation, particularly in the lower extremities. These negative consequences impose psychological and economic burdens on patients and countries. Oxidative stress plays a regulatory role throughout all four phases of cutaneous wound repair through multiple signaling cascades, including but not limited to the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE pathway and the PI3K/AKT pathway. In this review, we describe the relationships between oxidative stress and skin wound healing process, in order to provide the potential mechanisms for new options of treatment in skin wound healing via oxidative stress.

articles.title: Preclinical Evidence for Ligusticum chuanxiong-Derived Interventions in Experimental Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Animal Studies.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Ligusticum chuanxiong is a traditional medicinal herb widely used for conditions related to blood circulation, inflammation, and neurological dysfunction. Its extracts and major bioactive compounds, including tetramethylpyrazine and ferulic acid, have shown neuroprotective potential in experimental spinal cord injury (SCI). However, the broader preclinical evidence remains incompletely characterized. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and potential mechanisms of Ligusticum chuanxiong-derived interventions in experimental SCI METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP were systematically searched for animal studies evaluating Ligusticum chuanxiong-derived interventions in SCI models. The primary outcomes were BBB locomotor scores and inclined plane test performance. Secondary outcomes included inflammatory, oxidative stress, apoptotic, glial, and neuronal markers. Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool, and certainty of evidence using an adapted GRADE approach. RESULTS: Forty animal studies were included. Ligusticum chuanxiong-derived interventions were associated with improved BBB scores at 3, 7, 14, 21, and 28 days after SCI, as well as improved inclined plane test performance from 7 to 21 days after injury. Mechanistic outcomes showed reduced IL-1β, MDA, and TUNEL-positive cells, together with increased SOD levels, suggesting potential neuroprotective effects through anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and cell death-reducing mechanisms. At 28 days, immunofluorescence-based analyses indicated higher NeuN expression, whereas the pooled GFAP difference did not reach statistical significance; substantial heterogeneity limited certainty; caspase-3 expression was lower at 3 and 7 days, each based on three studies. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the BBB findings were generally robust, although potential publication bias or small-study effects were detected at several time points. An exploratory dose-time analysis of tetramethylpyrazine suggested that BBB effect sizes may increase over time, but the available evidence was insufficient to define an optimal dose. CONCLUSION: Ligusticum chuanxiong-derived interventions may improve motor recovery after experimental SCI, potentially through modulation of inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death. Further rigorously designed animal studies are needed to clarify active constituents, therapeutic windows, optimal dosing strategies, and translational potential.

articles.title: The genus Dendropanax (Araliaceae): A comprehensive review of the botany, traditional uses, phytochemistry, pharmacology, quality control, and economic importance.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: The genus Dendropanax is primary distributed in East Asia and tropical America, with some species being characteristic medicinal plants and economic crops in China and South Korea, exhibiting anti-inflammatory effects, alleviating rheumatic pain and migraine. However, reviews on the phytochemistry and pharmacology of this genus are scarce and unsystematic, hindering the rational application and in-depth development of these plants. AIMS OF THE REVIEW: This review comprehensively reviews the botany, traditional uses, phytochemistry, pharmacology, quality control, and economic importance of the genus, to provide a robust scientific foundation for its clinical application, quality control, and rational development. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic literature review of the genus Dendropanax was conducted using Chinese resources (e.g., books, CNKI, Wanfang, Weipu) and international databases (e.g., Web of Science, SciFinder, PubMed, ScienceDirect, Springer), followed by a systematic summary of the retrieved literature. RESULTS: The genus Dendropanax comprises ninety-seven accepted species, among which D. dentiger and D. proteus are traditional medicinal plants native to China, while D. morbiferus is a medicinal plant native to Korea. Since 1973, a total of one hundred and forty-seven chemical constituents have been isolated and identified from the genus Dendropanax, including forty-nine phenylpropanoids, twenty-one phenol derivatives, seventeen fatty acids and fatty alcohols, seventeen polyacetylenes, eleven flavonoids, nine triterpenoids, four sesquiterpenoids, six alkaloids, and thirteen others, across six species: D. dentiger (seventy-eight), D. proteus (sixteen), D. morbiferus (sixty-six), D. arboreus (seven), D. trifidus (four), and D. querceti (one). Additionally, seventy-eight, thirty-three, twenty-nine, and four volatile oil components were identified from D. arboreus, D. morbifera, D. gonatopodus, and D. capillaris, respectively. The genus Dendropanax exhibits a wide range of pharmacological activities, including anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, anti-tumor, hepatoprotective, anti-obesity, anti-diabetic, memory-improving, anti-hyperuricemic, neuroprotective, and renoprotective effects, but only involving six species: D. dentiger, D. proteus, D. morbiferus, D. arboreus, D. capillaris, and D. trifidus. Currently, only fingerprint analysis and HPLC content determination have been studied for D. dentiger and D. morbiferus, but no relevant quality standard protocols have been established. CONCLUSION: The Dendropanax genus exhibits diverse pharmacological activities and a diverse array of chemical constituents, but comprehensive research remains scarce and superficial, especially regarding the pharmacodynamic substances and mechanisms associated with traditional functions. Urgent investigations are required into the phytochemistry, pharmacology, and mechanism of Dendropanax species, as well as the development of robust, forward-looking, and practical quality standard protocols, to provide a scientific basis for their clinical application and rational development.

articles.title: Aldo-keto reductase family 1 member B10 in solid tumors: lipid metabolic reprogramming, immune remodeling, and targeted therapy.
articles.abstract: Aldo-keto reductase family 1 member B10 (AKR1B10), an NADPH-dependent aldo-keto reductase, has emerged as a context-dependent metabolic stress regulator with important implications for therapeutic resistance and tumor immune remodeling in solid tumors. By neutralizing lipid-derived aldehydes such as 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), AKR1B10 limits lipid-derived carbonyl stress and may reduce ferroptosis susceptibility in defined tumor contexts. It also stabilizes acetyl-CoA carboxylase α, thereby sustaining de novo lipogenesis (DNL). In addition, AKR1B10 has been linked to increased glycolysis-associated lactate production in specific tumor settings. This increase in lactate can promote histone lactylation-mediated epigenetic reprogramming. Together with reported associations between AKR1B10 and immune-cell infiltration or function, these metabolic effects may contribute to tumor immune remodeling in a context-dependent manner. Aberrant AKR1B10 expression has been associated with tumor progression and therapeutic resistance in several solid tumors, including hepatocellular carcinoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and cholangiocarcinoma. This review systematically examines the structural biology, transcriptional regulation, and tumor-intrinsic and microenvironmental functions of AKR1B10. It further evaluates its tumor-type-specific diagnostic and prognostic potential and discusses emerging inhibitor strategies. Nonetheless, key challenges remain, including the tissue-specific functional duality of AKR1B10, the demand for inhibitors selective over the structurally homologous AKR1B1, and limited causal evidence linking AKR1B10 to immune remodeling in tumors. Future research should integrate multimodal spatial omics, immunocompetent tumor models, and rational combination therapy designs to advance AKR1B10 from a metabolic enzyme into a clinically actionable target for precision oncology.

articles.title: CD14 in glioblastoma and temozolomide resistance: what the evidence does and does not support.
articles.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM), designated as central nervous system World Health Organization grade 4, is the most lethal adult brain tumor, with a median overall survival (OS) of 14.6 months despite resection, radiotherapy, and temozolomide (TMZ). The benefit of TMZ is largely confined to the 45 % of GBMs carrying a methylated O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter, where, in 206 assessable patients from the pivotal Phase III trial (reported in 2005), adding TMZ to radiotherapy extended median OS from 15.3 to 21.7 months, whereas MGMT-unmethylated tumors derived no significant benefit; these are historical estimates from a single trial subset. Resistance arises through MGMT-mediated repair of O6-methylguanine, MSH6 loss or mutation affecting mismatch repair, glioma stem cell repopulation, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment enriched with CD14+ myeloid cells, including tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), monocytes, and monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells. CD14 is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored co-receptor for Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), expressed constitutively on monocytes, macrophages, and microglia and also by a subset of glioma cells. Because CD14 has no intracellular domain, it cannot signal independently of a partner receptor; CD14-dependent signaling through TLR4/MD-2 has been proposed to contribute to nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) activation, pro-survival transcription, MGMT-related resistance pathways, and immunosuppressive myeloid polarization, although no study has shown this in glioma cells, the link to TMZ resistance remains hypothetical, and CD14 alone does not define an M2-like TAM phenotype. This review synthesizes over 50 publications across CD14 biology in the brain, CD14 expression across the immune and tumor-cell landscape of GBM, CD14-associated inflammatory signaling, TMZ resistance mechanisms, CD14-related influences on TMZ sensitivity, and candidate therapeutic strategies. Of those strategies, only IC14 (atibuclimab) targets CD14 directly; TLR4, NF-κB, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 and colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor inhibition, TAM repolarization, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibition, and checkpoint blockade act on the partner receptor, on shared downstream nodes or on the CD14-enriched myeloid compartment, and are therefore described as CD14-associated rather than CD14-targeted. CD14+ myeloid populations are associated with aggressive GBM biology, whereas the proposed glioma-cell-intrinsic CD14 → TLR4/MD-2 → NF-κB → MGMT cascade rests on a single 2003 expression dataset and has never been tested by CD14 loss-of-function, gain-of-function, rescue or lineage-specific in vivo experiments. The purpose of this review is to document that gap and to specify the experiments that would close it, not to advocate CD14 as a therapeutic target.

articles.title: Antibiotic-derived peptides delivered by nanocarriers as multifunctional pharmacological modulators in chronic wound healing.
articles.abstract: Chronic wounds, particularly those associated with diabetes and metabolic disorders, represent a persistent therapeutic challenge characterized by sustained inflammation, microbial colonization, oxidative imbalance, and impaired angiogenesis. Current pharmacological management relies heavily on antimicrobial agents; however, conventional antibiotics primarily address infection and exert limited influence on host pathways governing tissue repair. Recent studies indicate that peptide derivatives originating from antibiotic scaffolds retain membrane-targeting properties while also interacting with immune, redox, and cellular signaling networks relevant to wound resolution. This review examines antibiotic-derived peptides as pharmacologically active molecules whose therapeutic profile can be reshaped through nanocarrier-based delivery. Liposomal and lipid-based nanocarriers are discussed not only as drug transport systems but also as modulators of pharmacokinetics, spatial distribution, and microenvironmental exposure within the wound bed. Such systems enable sustained local presentation of peptides, potentially influencing macrophage polarization, cytokine balance, angiogenic signaling, and extracellular matrix remodeling in addition to antimicrobial effects. By integrating evidence from peptide pharmacology, wound pathophysiology, and controlled-release science, we evaluate how structural optimization and carrier design jointly determine biological activity in chronic wound settings. Key challenges, including proteolytic instability, dose localization, safety considerations, and translational scalability are analyzed to define the boundaries of clinical applicability. This perspective highlights the repositioning of antibiotic-derived peptides from infection-focused agents toward multifunctional regulators of tissue repair, providing a mechanistic basis for future pharmacological development in chronic wound therapy.

articles.title: Engineering the skin barrier: reprogramming stratum corneum structure for next-generation dermal drug delivery.
articles.abstract: The stratum corneum (SC) is now increasingly recognized as a dynamic regulatory interface, rather than a passive barrier, for dermal drug delivery. Permeability is controlled by coordinated lipid organization, corneocyte maturation, hydration control, enzymatic processing and junctional signaling, all of which are altered in inflammatory, genetic and age-related skin disorders. Traditional methods for penetration enhancement mainly function by disrupting this architecture, but this non-specific disruption can compromise barrier integrity, cause increased irritation and limit its use in repeated or long-term therapy. This sets up an obvious need for techniques that control, not just break, the skin barrier. In this review, we put forward the idea of engineering the skin barrier as a mechanism-driven strategy for reversible and targeted control of SC permeability and repair. It combines current knowledge on barrier biology with advances in biomimetic materials, responsive delivery systems, extracellular vesicles, smart hydrogels, organotypic models and computational design, and assesses how barrier function can be modulated with greater spatial, temporal and disease-specific precision. Special attention is paid to the translational gaps that currently limit this field, including proof of reversibility, standardized barrier assessment, interpatient variability, and regulatory definition. Skin barrier engineering is typically framed as a safer and more flexible paradigm for next-generation personalized dermal therapeutics.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics of Antibiotics in Prostatitis and Lower Urinary Tract Infections in Men: A Critical Scoping Review of the Published Concentration Data.
articles.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most frequent community-acquired infections in men and are associated with substantial morbidity. This review maps the available evidence on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) of antibiotics in the human male urogenital tract and appraises the methodological features that govern its interpretation. We conducted a scoping review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), of the physicochemical properties of major antibiotic classes and of the available evidence on their penetration into male urogenital tissues and fluids. Data quantity and quality vary considerably across antibiotics and study designs. β-Lactams reach effective concentrations in prostate tissue, testis, and urine, but achieve only limited levels in prostatic secretions; data for bladder tissue and seminal fluid remain scarce. Fosfomycin achieves therapeutic concentrations in prostate tissue, prostatic secretions, seminal fluid, bladder tissue, and urine, with no testicular data. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole provides effective levels in prostate tissue, testis, and urine, while only trimethoprim attains adequate concentrations in prostatic secretions and seminal fluid; data for bladder tissue are lacking. Fluoroquinolones achieved therapeutic concentrations in all relevant compartments, including prostate tissue, prostatic secretions, seminal fluid, testis, bladder tissue, and urine. Evidence for other antibiotic classes remains limited. The available evidence is unevenly distributed across compartments and antibiotic classes, and is constrained by the use of tissue homogenates, total-drug measurement, and single-timepoint sampling in largely uninfected patients. This review defines the boundaries of what can currently be inferred and identifies where compartment-specific data are lacking.

articles.title: Steroidogenic potency and therapeutic selectivity of azole enantiomers in vitro.
Is the cardio-immune microenvironment a convergent hub of cardiovascular toxicity across novel anticancer therapies?
articles.abstract: Novel anticancer therapies have transformed oncology but have also expanded the spectrum of cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity, including myocarditis, ventricular dysfunction, hypertension, vascular inflammation, thrombosis, arrhythmias, fibrosis, and heart failure. In cardio-oncology, the cardio-immune microenvironment provides a useful framework for integrating cardiovascular toxicity across immune checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T cell therapy and other T-cell-redirecting therapies, HER2-directed therapies, VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates, radiotherapy-containing regimens, and combination treatments. This Review discusses the cardio- immune microenvironment as a tissue-level network in which immune cells, cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, vascular cells, fibroblasts, soluble mediators, and extracellular-matrix cues interact during injury and repair. Rather than proposing a universal immune origin for all cardiotoxic effects, we distinguish three routes by which novel anticancer treatments may enter this network: immune initiation, systemic inflammatory translation, and primary cardiomyocyte, endothelial, vascular, or payload-related injury followed by immune amplification and remodeling. We define mechanistically meaningful convergence as engagement of a shared downstream cellular-molecular response module by therapies with distinct proximal mechanisms, while distinguishing such convergence from nonspecific injury-repair responses. We organize the cardio-immune framework around five mechanistic domains: immune tolerance breakdown, cytokine-driven systemic inflammation, sterile danger sensing, myeloid and stromal reprogramming, and endothelial-immune coupling. We further discuss how these mechanisms may inform therapy-specific risk stratification, biomarker interpretation, imaging surveillance, mechanism-guided intervention, and multi-omics approaches in precision cardio-oncology. This context-dependent framework may help clarify why distinct anticancer therapies can produce overlapping cardiovascular phenotypes while preserving therapy-specific mechanisms and clinical management priorities.

articles.title: Hepatoprotective mechanism of tauroursodeoxycholic acid and its therapeutic potential in liver diseases.
articles.abstract: Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is a natural hydrophilic secondary bile acid that acts as an effective chemical chaperone and exerts dramatically hepatoprotective effects. It alleviates endoplasmic reticulum stress (ERS), regulates the unfolded protein response (UPR), suppresses inflammatory responses, reduces oxidative stress, and inhibits hepatocyte apoptosis. In addition, TUDCA maintains bile acid metabolism homeostasis and modulates the gut-liver axis, showing significant therapeutic potential in multiple liver disorders, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), cholestatic liver injury, liver fibrosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI). Despite promising preclinical evidence, the specific crosstalk between TUDCA and the gut microbiota remains largely unclear, and high-quality clinical evidence supporting its translation into clinical practice is still limited. This narrative review summarises the molecular targets and signaling pathways of TUDCA, discusses current research gaps, and provides a theoretical foundation for its rational clinical application and future mechanistic studies.

articles.title: Natural products and extracellular vesicle-associated miRNA networks in perianal infectious wound healing: a critical ethnopharmacological appraisal.
articles.abstract: Perianal infectious wounds form a contaminated, moist, mechanically disturbed repair niche that differs from standard cutaneous wounds. This critical narrative review evaluates whether natural-product pharmacology and extracellular vesicle (EV)-associated miRNA biology can be linked credibly in this setting. A structured PubMed search updated through 29 September 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar citation tracking, identified direct human perianal studies, anatomically relevant and infection-relevant animal studies, and mechanistically relevant in vitro and in silico evidence. Core studies were appraised on two separate axes: clinical/model proximity and methodological credibility, including material identity and taxonomic validity, chemical characterization, exposure, comparators and controls, model fidelity, EV characterization, causal miRNA evidence, and assay-interference risk. Direct human ethnopharmacological evidence now includes several randomized postoperative studies, although blinding, material standardization, comparator quality, endpoint selection, and mechanistic depth remain heterogeneous. Early-phase mesenchymal stromal cell EV studies provide perianal feasibility and fistula-closure signals without controlled comparative efficacy. A 2025 Wugu Qilin study provides direct human treatment-associated evidence from wound-fluid vesicle-enriched miRNA profiling involving miR-93-3p/EIF4EBP1, but it did not demonstrate EV-mediated transfer to recipient cells. Astragaloside IV-conditioned endothelial progenitor-cell EV studies provide stronger nonperianal cargo-level evidence, whereas curcumin-loaded macrophage EVs primarily support vesicle-assisted delivery. No study establishes the full causal sequence from chemically defined natural-product exposure through rigorously characterized EV cargo alteration and transfer of a defined miRNA to a necessary recipient-cell effect and improved healing in an anatomically faithful perianal model. Direct clinical and translational evidence is therefore present, but the natural product-EV-miRNA mechanism remains unproven; the most immediate needs are material standardization, clinically derived wound-fluid EV profiling, mixed-biofilm models, causal cargo perturbation, assay-interference controls, and stage-adapted local delivery.

articles.title: Compartment-specific roles of gasdermin D and E in photoreceptor degeneration: evidence and pharmacological implications.
articles.abstract: Photoreceptor degeneration arises from diverse genetic and acquired insults, yet oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and sterile inflammation repeatedly converge on membrane injury and irreversible cell loss. Inflammasome activation is frequently described as retinal pyroptosis, although upstream markers alone neither establish gasdermin-dependent lysis nor identify the executing cell. Rather than treating retinal pyroptosis as a single cell-autonomous pathway, we distinguish a myeloid gasdermin D (GSDMD) inflammatory relay from a photoreceptor-intrinsic gasdermin E (GSDME) lytic amplification program and evaluate potential interventions according to direct retinal evidence, cellular specificity, and translational readiness. GSDMD is best supported in microglia and subretinal macrophages, where inflammasome-caspase-1 signaling promotes cytokine and extracellular-vesicle release and can worsen secondary photoreceptor injury. Recent evidence in TREM2-deficient rd10 retina further supports GSDMD as a functional disease modifier, while remaining context specific. By contrast, GSDME has direct loss-of-function support in all-trans-retinal overload, in which caspase-3-dependent cleavage increases membrane rupture and is associated with mitochondrial oxidative burden and ferroptotic susceptibility. We compare NLRP3/caspase-1, interleukin-1, GSDMD pore, GSDME, and redox-directed strategies against five translational gates: target engagement, ocular exposure, cell specificity, delivery feasibility, and safety. This evidence-graded framework identifies promising pharmacological entry points while preserving the distinction between mechanistic plausibility and retinal target readiness.

articles.title: Targeting neddylation in cancer: molecular mechanisms, translational advances, and therapeutic challenges.
articles.abstract: Neddylation is a ubiquitin-like post-translational modification that regulates cullin-RING ligases and selected non-cullin substrates involved in cell-cycle progression, DNA replication licensing, DNA-damage repair, apoptosis, hypoxic signaling, inflammatory responses, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, metabolic adaptation, and immune regulation. Many tumors rely on aberrant neddylation-dependent protein turnover to sustain proliferation, survival, metastatic plasticity, and therapeutic resistance, making this pathway a compelling anticancer target. This review outlines the molecular architecture of the NEDD8 cascade, encompassing NEDD8 activation, E2-mediated conjugation, E3/co-E3-facilitated ligation, deneddylation, and the central role of cullin-RING ligases as oncogenic effectors. It also examines the principal classes of neddylation-pathway inhibitors, including the first-in-class NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924, newer NAE inhibitors such as TAS4464, emerging UBE2M- and UBE2F-directed approaches, DCN1/DCUN1-targeted inhibitors, and natural product-derived or other experimental compounds. Preclinical evidence across hematologic malignancies, gastrointestinal and genitourinary cancers, thoracic and head-and-neck tumors, brain tumors, and pediatric cancers indicates that neddylation inhibition can suppress tumor growth and enhance responses to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, apoptosis-targeted agents, proteasome inhibition, autophagy modulation, and immunotherapy. Nevertheless, clinical translation remains constrained by inadequate patient selection, context-dependent substrate accumulation, adaptive resistance, complex immune effects, and limited therapeutic windows.
